title: Event perception: a mind-brain perspective
authors: Jeffrey M. Zacks, Nicole K. Speer, Khena M. Swallow, Todd S. Braver, Jeremy R. Reynolds
key_findings: Proposes Event Segmentation Theory (EST): perceptual systems continuously predict what happens next; a transient rise in prediction error is perceived as an event boundary
Event perception depends on sensory cues and on knowledge structures about event parts and actors' goals/plans
Boundaries regulate attention and memory
practical_applications: Scene/beat breaks in a carousel or clip should coincide with a real change (goal, place, character) so the viewer's boundary and ours line up
limitations: Read abstract only (Europe PMC); neural claims are model-level

title: The Construction of Situation Models in Narrative Comprehension: An Event-Indexing Model
authors: Rolf A. Zwaan, Mark C. Langston, Arthur C. Graesser
key_findings: Events are the focal points of situation models and are connected in memory along five dimensions: time, space, protagonist, causality, intentionality
Verb-clustering task supported the model
practical_applications: Use the five indices as the minimum fields of a continuity record per episode
limitations: Abstract only (OpenAlex); simple text narratives, not film

title: Segmentation in reading and film comprehension
authors: Jeffrey M. Zacks, Nicole K. Speer, Jeremy R. Reynolds
key_findings: Changes in characters, locations, object interactions and goals predict where readers/viewers mark event boundaries, in both texts and films
Clauses with event boundaries are read more slowly; situational change partly mediates this
Predictability of incoming information may influence reading rate and segmentation
practical_applications: Each situational change costs processing; stack few changes per slide/shot in short-form
limitations: Abstract only (Europe PMC)

title: Event boundaries in perception affect memory encoding and updating
authors: Khena M. Swallow, Jeffrey M. Zacks, Richard A. Abrams
key_findings: Objects present when an event boundary occurred were better recognized 5 s later
Memory contents appear to be updated at event boundaries
practical_applications: Place the hero prop / key clue on screen AT a boundary (scene change, reveal) to make it memorable
limitations: Abstract only; lab movie clips of goal-directed activity

title: Event Boundaries in Memory and Cognition
authors: Gabriel A. Radvansky, Jeffrey M. Zacks
key_findings: Outlines the Event Horizon Model: current event model highly available, prior event models less available; boundaries affect working and long-term memory and event model updating
practical_applications: After a scene change viewers lose easy access to details of the previous scene: re-show critical info after cuts
limitations: Abstract only; doorway-forgetting effect not found in every experiment (per secondary reports)

title: Segmentation in the perception and memory of events
authors: Christopher A. Kurby, Jeffrey M. Zacks
key_findings: (Per search summary) EST: segmentation is a side effect of trying to anticipate upcoming information; posterior temporal, parietal and lateral frontal cortex show transient increases at boundaries
practical_applications: Background review for EST
limitations: Only search snippet read; PMC blocked bots

title: The Scene Perception & Event Comprehension Theory (SPECT) Applied to Visual Narratives
authors: Lester C. Loschky, Adam M. Larson, Tim J. Smith, Joseph P. Magliano
key_findings: Distinguishes front-end processes (attentional selection, information extraction within fixations) from back-end processes (event model construction in working memory and episodic memory)
Medium-specific differences (picture stories vs film) likely vary these processes
practical_applications: Carousels are picture stories: each slide must let the eye find the key info in 1-2 fixations (front end) before the story can update (back end)
limitations: Abstract only (Wiley PDF returned 403); Topics in Cognitive Science (online 2019)

title: The relative roles of visuospatial and linguistic working memory systems in generating inferences during visual narrative comprehension
authors: Joseph P. Magliano, Adam M. Larson, Karyn Higgs, Lester C. Loschky
key_findings: When a bridging-event image is omitted from a picture story, viewers look longer at the end-state image (online bridging inference); think-aloud protocols contained more inferred actions
Both visuospatial and linguistic WM loads attenuated the inference effect (shared systems); articulatory suppression did not
Picture viewing times are sensitive to mental model construction
practical_applications: Omitting an easily inferable action between slides engages viewers but costs processing time: give the end-state slide dwell time and never omit non-inferable steps
limitations: Lab picture stories, student samples

title: Understanding Moment-to-Moment Processing of Visual Narratives
authors: John P. Hutson, Joseph P. Magliano, Lester C. Loschky
key_findings: Eye-tracking test of SPECT: when inferable actions are missing, viewing time on the next image rises; tests computational-load vs visual-search accounts
practical_applications: Design the image after a gap so the inference cue is easy to find
limitations: Abstract only

title: Visual narrative comprehension: Universal or not?
authors: Neil Cohn
key_findings: Sequential images are not universally transparent: comprehension requires fluency acquired through exposure and practice
Cross-cultural reports (Papua New Guinea, Aboriginal Australian, Kenya) of people reading each image as its own story; familiarity with comics improved sequential reading
Fluency matures developmentally and can be asymmetric for comprehension vs production
practical_applications: Do not assume every audience reads a carousel as one sequence; add continuity cues (same characters, same place, slide numbers) for less comic-fluent audiences
limitations: Review; many cross-cultural sources are old and small

title: Exploring the Effects of Violating the 180-Degree Rule on Film Viewing Preferences
authors: George V. Kachkovski, Daniil Vasilyev, Michael Kuk, Alan Kingstone, Chris N. H. Street
key_findings: Naive viewers detected 180-degree violations (responded to .42 of violating cuts vs .08 of matched control cuts)
Violations can confuse and disorient viewers
Violations did not change liking: viewers were as likely to prefer the violating video
practical_applications: Keep screen sides for clarity, but a single slip is a comprehension risk, not a liking disaster
limitations: Read OSF preprint; Communication Research 2019; short clips, student samples

title: Spatiotemporal jump detection during continuous film viewing
authors: Aditya Upadhyayula, John M. Henderson
key_findings: Viewers instructed to detect disruptions missed jumps in minute-long movie clips about 10-30% of the time depending on jump size
Detection about 10% lower for forward jumps than backward jumps
practical_applications: Forward time skips (ellipsis) are tolerated; backward jumps (flashbacks) are noticed more and need clear marking
limitations: Abstract only (JOV); related 2024 APP paper not read

title: The Role of Cliffhangers in Serial Entertainment: An Experiment on Cliffhangers' Effects on Enjoyment, Arousal, and Intention to Continue Watching
authors: Dominique S. Wirz, Alexander Ort, Bjorn Rasch, Andreas Fahr
key_findings: Lab experiment N=133, 3-4 episodes of a drama ending with or without a cliffhanger; self-report plus electrodermal activity and cortisol
Cliffhangers raised arousal but did not increase enjoyment or intention to continue watching compared with mere unfinished narration
Authors note cliffhangers might matter more for immediate continuation within a session
practical_applications: Do not rely on a cliffhanger as the main retention tool; an unresolved overall arc may do the same work
limitations: Read accepted-manuscript PDF (University of Fribourg repository); journal per search: Psychology of Popular Media; one series, Swiss sample

title: Investigating Responses to Narrative Cliffhangers Using Affective Disposition Theory
authors: Katherine Schibler, Lindsay Hahn, Melanie C. Green
key_findings: Two experiments (N=202, N=273) with written narratives: cliffhanger readers desired a future installment more than readers of protagonist-victory endings (both studies) and antagonist-victory endings (Study 2)
No significant differences in enjoyment or suspense
practical_applications: Cliffhangers may raise desire for the next part without costing enjoyment - complements Wirz2022's null on intention
limitations: Abstract only; written stories, not video

title: Antecedents and Effects of Parasocial Relationships: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Riva Tukachinsky, Nathan Walter, Camille J. Saucier
key_findings: (Per search summary of abstract) k=120 over four decades; PSR and PSI only moderately correlated (distinct constructs)
PSRs a stronger predictor of media involvement
Social deficiencies (e.g., loneliness) not significantly related to PSRs
practical_applications: Recurring characters build relationship-like attachment that predicts involvement - protect their consistency
limitations: Only abstract-level snippets read

title: Horton and Wohl Revisited: Exploring Viewers' Experience of Parasocial Interaction
authors: Tilo Hartmann, Charlotte Goldhoorn
key_findings: 2x2 experiment N=198: bodily and verbal addressing by a TV performer intensified parasocial experience; stronger PSI led to greater enjoyment
practical_applications: A recurring narrator addressing the viewer strengthens PSI; a faceless duo who never address the viewer relies on observed relationship instead
limitations: Abstract only; real performer, not fictional character

title: Speaking of Soap Operas (ch. 'A Reader-Oriented Poetics of the Soap Opera')
authors: Robert C. Allen
key_findings: Soap opera is predicated on the impossibility of final closure; trades a telos for overlapping 'mini-closures'
Its uniqueness is paradigmatic complexity: a community of 40+ interrelated characters; who a character is depends on their place in the network
Interepisodic redundancy keeps non-daily viewers up to date; intraepisodic redundancy (same news passed character to character) is meaningful to experienced viewers because of relationship history
Soap characters have histories and memories; reading time spans years, so long-time viewers read scenes against decades of history
Relationships can be transformed by revelations ('a discovered birth certificate')
practical_applications: For long-running series keep a relationship registry; repeat key facts for newcomers by passing them through different characters
limitations: 1985 US daytime soaps; humanities analysis, not experimental
license: copyrighted (UNC Press); scan hosted by worldradiohistory.com

title: Narrative Complexity in Contemporary American Television
authors: Jason Mittell
key_findings: (Bibliographic; per secondary summary) narrative complexity as a redefinition of episodic forms under the influence of serial narration; Velvet Light Trap 58, 29-40
practical_applications: Background for the episodic/serial hybrid
limitations: Full text blocked (Project MUSE verification)

title: The Legendary Star Wars Expanded Universe Turns a New Page
authors: StarWars.com / Lucasfilm
key_findings: 25 Apr 2014: the six films and The Clone Wars are the canon all stories must align with; prior Expanded Universe reissued under the 'Legends' banner
Lucasfilm formed a story group to 'oversee and coordinate all Star Wars creative development'
Creators keep full access to EU material (Rebels reused the Inquisitor, ISB, Sienar from 1980s RPG material)
practical_applications: Canon tiers: declare what is canon vs archived; archived material stays a quarry for new canon
limitations: Corporate announcement; motives partly commercial

title: How The Lucasfilm Story Group Figures Out The Star Wars Canon
authors: Germain Lussier (SlashFilm)
key_findings: Report of Star Wars Celebration 2015 'One Big Story' panel (Pablo Hidalgo, Leland Chee); group headed by Kiri Hart
Plans major story beats years ahead; checks pitches fit; may say 'come back in six years'; commissions stories; approval for 'authenticity' does not always mean canon (e.g., multi-ending games)
Hidalgo: Boba Fett is 'both simultaneously alive and dead in the Sarlacc pit until a story pulls him out'
practical_applications: Keep a list of deliberately undetermined facts; separate 'on-brand' from 'canon'
limitations: Journalistic report of a panel

title: Building Imaginary Worlds: An Interview with Mark J. P. Wolf (Part Three)
authors: Henry Jenkins (interviewer), Mark J. P. Wolf
key_findings: Basic infrastructures of a world: maps (space), timelines (time), genealogies (characters); also nature, culture, language, mythology, philosophy, narrative
Fans police continuity - a sign they care; creators should be clear about what is canonical

Secondary belief needs consistency; fans explain away minor inconsistencies; quality of detail matters as much as quantity; 'there are always ways of expanding a world that do not disrupt its consistency'
practical_applications: Registry structure = map + timeline + genealogy/relationship graph
limitations: Interview; author's own summary of his book

title: Sanderson's Second Law
authors: Brandon Sanderson
key_findings: 'Limitations > Powers': characters and magic are interesting for what they cannot do
Costs can be abstract (gradual madness) or concrete (ingredients); too severe a cost means the magic is rarely used
practical_applications: Every world rule records its limit/cost; character 'never' lists matter as much as abilities
limitations: Craft opinion of a novelist; first printed in Leading Edge #61

title: Sanderson's Third Law of Magic
authors: Brandon Sanderson
key_findings: 'Expand what you already have before you add something new' - deep rather than wide worldbuilding
Extrapolate, interconnect, streamline; example of cutting an underused character and giving the role to others
practical_applications: Before adding a new character/place to a long series, check whether an existing one can carry the role
limitations: Craft opinion; posting date not shown on page

title: On Fairy Stories (commentary on Tolkien's essay)
authors: Verlyn Flieger (Tolkien Estate website)
key_findings: Essay is Tolkien's definitive statement of 'sub-creation'; the power of words to create a Secondary World
Lecture March 1939 (Andrew Lang Lecture, St Andrews); expanded in Essays Presented to Charles Williams (1947); Tree and Leaf (1964); expanded edition by Flieger & Anderson (2008)
Fantasy offers Recovery, Escape, Consolation; 'eucatastrophe'
practical_applications: Historical anchor for 'sub-creation' and 'Secondary World' vocabulary
limitations: Secondary commentary; did not cover the Secondary Belief passage

title: Regeneration & Rebirth: Anatomy of the Franchise Reboot
authors: William Proctor
key_findings: A reboot is a franchise-specific concept: it disavows prior continuity and restarts from 'year one'; a single film cannot be rebooted, only remade
DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths (1986) destroyed the multiverse to escape a convoluted, contradictory continuity; Infinite Crisis (2006) partly reversed it
Uses Hills' 'hyperdiegesis' for a vast, consistent storyworld
practical_applications: Options when continuity breaks: fix, retcon, soft reboot, hard reboot - each with a different cost
limitations: Film/TV studies essay (Scope, Nottingham); qualitative

title: Retcon Game: Retroactive Continuity and the Hyperlinking of America
authors: Andrew J. Friedenthal
key_findings: (Per publisher/catalogue summary) treats retconning as a force shaping how Americans view history and culture; chapter 'Crisis Control' on DC's unified comic universe
practical_applications: Background on retcon as a deliberate tool
limitations: Only catalogue/search snippets read; year not confirmed

title: Transmedia 202: Further Reflections
authors: Henry Jenkins
key_findings: Contrasts continuity (consistent world) with multiplicity (same characters told differently, alternate versions)
Seriality = chunking and dispersal with hooks; most transmedia is serial but not all serials are transmedia
Worldbuilding as one function of additive comprehension
practical_applications: Mark spin-offs/what-ifs explicitly as 'multiplicity' so they don't contaminate canon
limitations: Blog essay

title: StoryDiffusion: Consistent Self-Attention for Long-Range Image and Video Generation
authors: Yupeng Zhou, Daquan Zhou, Ming-Ming Cheng, Jiashi Feng, Qibin Hou
key_findings: Training-free Consistent Self-Attention shares sampled tokens across images in a batch to keep subjects consistent; sliding window for long stories; Semantic Motion Predictor for video
NeurIPS 2024 spotlight
practical_applications: Batch-generate all panels of one story together when the tool allows
limitations: Abstract/HTML only; consistency is within one generated sequence

title: ViStoryBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Story Visualization
authors: Cailin Zhuang, Ailin Huang, Yaoqi Hu, Jingwei Wu, Wei Cheng, Jiaqi Liao, et al.
key_findings: 80 stories, 344 characters, 509 reference images, 10 styles, 1,317 shots; 30+ configurations incl. StoryDiffusion, UNO, OmniGen2, GPT-4o, Gemini, Seedream, Sora2 and commercial tools
Clear trade-off between character consistency and prompt adherence/creativity; image references raise consistency but limit novelty
A copy-paste baseline scores well on some consistency metrics but poorly on prompt alignment -> 'Copy-Paste Rate' metric
Models often add or omit characters (OCCM metric)
Self-consistency metric correlated best with human ratings (Kendall tau .50); aesthetics weakest
practical_applications: QC must check identity AND whether the panel does what the script says; watch for missing/extra characters in two-character scenes
limitations: Read first ~100k characters of HTML v4 (main results); benchmark lacks background-reference and video metrics; vendor versions change fast

title: The "Phi"
authors: Phya Anuman Rajadhon (ed. Margaret Coughlin)
key_findings: 'Phi' once covered good and bad supernatural beings; after Khmer/Hindu influence good phi became thevada and phi narrowed to ghost/evil spirit
Chao phi: guardian spirits of a place, with shrines; addressed as chao phaw/chao mae
Phi ruan: a dead family member who stays invisibly in the house and looks after the family; a sacred, tabooed place in the house; the family asks its permission on important occasions
A person who dies a violent death becomes phi tai hong; a woman dying in childbirth becomes phi tai thang klom; such corpses customarily buried, not cremated
practical_applications: Ghost rules for a Thai ghost series can be grounded in documented Thai belief (phi ruan = protective ancestor presence) instead of Western ghost tropes
limitations: 1954 folklorist's account of mainly Central Thai belief; regional variation; beliefs have changed since

title: Western-styled Buildings in Bangkok: Shophouses and Commercial Buildings in Khlong Khu Mueang Doem Canal Area
authors: Pichit Angkasuparakul
key_findings: Shophouses along the former city-moat canal developed after the Bowring Treaty and new road construction (from around Rama V); Western ornament on facades, gradually moving to modern style; land owned by elites or the state enabled steady building
practical_applications: External-realism anchor for a canal-side shophouse setting: period cues must match era
limitations: Abstract only (English); Thai-language article; Damrong Journal 24(2)

title: How Marketers Can Harness the Power of 'Callbacks'
authors: Duke Fuqua Insights (on research by Yuji Winet and colleagues)
key_findings: Callback = something familiar returns in a new context that changes its meaning
5,500+ jokes from Netflix specials: callbacks drew ~8 s of laughter/applause vs ~3 s
748 participants, 17 commercials: after two weeks callback ads remembered better than ads shown twice
LLM-generated callback score correlated with IMDb ratings/box office (correlational)
practical_applications: Running gags should return in a new context (callback), not as identical repetition
limitations: Unpublished 'ongoing research' described in a university press article; one brand's ads; LLM-rated scores

title: Assistant Script Editor - Coronation Street (job listing)
authors: ITV / ProductionBase
key_findings: (Per search summary) role reads scripts to keep established characters treated consistently; requires knowledge of storyline, plots and characters; related ITV listings: script supervisor notes continuity, makeup continuity across filming blocks
practical_applications: Real soap productions assign continuity to named roles (script editing, script supervision, makeup)
limitations: Search snippet only; job listings

title: Sanderson's First Law
authors: Brandon Sanderson
key_findings: 'An author's ability to solve conflict with magic is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to how well the reader understands said magic.'
Soft systems (vague rules) create wonder and should rarely solve problems; hard systems (clear rules) can solve problems; most writers sit between; prefers rules, costs and laws.
Don't add convenient new powers or laws to fit one situation.
practical_applications: Any special rule in a series (immunity, ghosts visiting at 2 am, a glasses 'power') may only resolve a plot if it was set up earlier.
limitations: Craft essay by a novelist; tier D, not science.

title: Tablets of Stone or DNA? TV series bibles
authors: Ian W. Macdonald
key_findings: Journal of Screenwriting 9(1), 3-23 (accepted manuscript read). Bible lengths vary widely: from a 3-page treatment worked up to 10 pages, 5-8 and 20-25 pages, to 50-60 pages (House of Cards) and 79 pages (The Wire); writers define bibles vaguely.

Types: selling bible, writer's bible, season bible (with storyline wall chart), production bible codifying 'case law', format bible for international sales; a 'walking bible' person may hold the memory.
'Less a tablet of stone, and more like a DNA code'; always ask 'which version?'.

Typical contents: premise/concept, place, locations, character biographies, rationale, structure & style, research, production detail (case law), episode storylines. Level of detail depends on what is culturally familiar versus new.
practical_applications: Structure for STORY_BIBLE_TEMPLATE.md: DNA layer + case-law layer + episode layer, versioned.
limitations: Small UK sample of writers and bibles.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: range wording corrected (separate examples).

title: What is the Holocron?
authors: Leland Chee
key_findings: Lucasfilm's continuity database, created January 2000 (FileMaker per other sources) when licensed products needed to track new material; before it, lore lived in binders called 'bibles'.
Tracks stories, discrepancies, images, stats, pronunciations, translations, costume variations and behind-the-scenes info; plus style guides, timelines, spelling dictionaries, quote banks and maps.
Over 55,000 entries in 2012 (19,000+ characters, 2,900 species, 5,300 worlds).
practical_applications: Even a tiny studio benefits from one database of entities with IDs, a discrepancy log and a spelling list (Thai/English names).
limitations: Official blog post by the database keeper; 2012 snapshot.

title: Complex TV: The Poetics of Contemporary Television Storytelling - chapter 'Orienting Paratexts'
authors: Jason Mittell
key_findings: NYU Press 2015. Chapter abstract: digital-era viewers use paratexts (wikis such as Lostpedia, infographics, character charts) to make sense of complex TV's temporality, characters, plot and spatial orientation.
Foregrounds 'forensic fandom' and 'drillability' as modes of spectatorship.

Comprehension chapter (Scalar companion abstract): serials keep viewers oriented across viewing practices; play with knowledge gaps between characters and viewers; trigger or exploit fading viewer memory for surprise
practical_applications: For serial content, publish orienting aids (recap card, character card, map) - the audience will build them anyway.
limitations: Only chapter abstract and examples read.

title: Situation models in language comprehension and memory
authors: Rolf A. Zwaan, Gabriel A. Radvansky
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 123(2), 162-185. Situation models are indexed on time, space, causation, intentionality and protagonist.
Readers notice when a protagonist's action contradicts an earlier trait (elevated reading times), citing Albrecht & O'Brien.
practical_applications: World facts the audience tracks automatically: when, where, why, goals, who; these are the consistency priorities of a world bible.
limitations: Text comprehension research; video transfer by analogy.

title: Edit Blindness: The relationship between attention and global change blindness in dynamic scenes
authors: Tim J. Smith, John M. Henderson
key_findings: Journal of Eye Movement Research 2(2):6. Viewers asked to detect edits in excerpts of seven feature films while eye-tracked.
Overall 15.8% of edits were missed even when viewers were explicitly looking for them.
Within-scene cuts (25.1% missed) and match-action cuts (32.4% missed) produced more edit blindness than between-scene cuts (9.4%) and gaze-match cuts (10.9%).
Blinks coincided with very few missed cuts (about 1%); most edit blindness is attributed to attention being absorbed by the narrative, not to blinks/saccades.
Cut detection time averaged 489 ms.
practical_applications: Cut on action and keep spatial continuity within a scene to make cuts invisible; between-scene jumps are noticed and should be signalled deliberately.
In 2D puppet/AI clips, a match-action cut is a cheap way to hide a change of generated image.
limitations: Small sample of films and participants; viewers were instructed to detect edits, so free-viewing blindness is likely higher.

title: The impact of continuity editing in narrative film on event segmentation
authors: Joseph P. Magliano, Jeffrey M. Zacks
key_findings: fMRI + segmentation of a commercial film; three degrees of continuity at edits: continuous in space/time/action; discontinuous in space or time but continuous in action; discontinuous in action
Discontinuities in action had the biggest effect on event segmentation; space/time discontinuities had minor effects
Specialized higher-order mechanisms maintain continuity of action across spatiotemporal discontinuities
practical_applications: Viewers chunk a story by action; a jump in location/time inside the same action reads as continuous, while breaking the action reads as a new event.
limitations: Abstract read via OpenAlex (upgraded from search_summary); one film

title: Training-Free Consistent Text-to-Image Generation (ConsiStory)
authors: Yoad Tewel, Omri Kaduri, Rinon Gal, Yoni Kasten, Lior Wolf, Gal Chechik, Yuval Atzmon
key_findings: SIGGRAPH 2024 (TOG). Generates a consistent subject across a batch of images by sharing internal activations (subject-driven shared attention, feature injection) with no optimisation step.
Claims state-of-the-art subject consistency and text alignment versus baselines; prior methods need per-subject optimisation or large-scale pre-training and struggle with multi-subject scenes.
practical_applications: Tool class 'batch-shared attention': generate all frames of one episode in one batch to keep the subject aligned.
limitations: Abstract only; consistency holds within a batch, not necessarily across separate sessions/episodes.
